findings.title: Ethnicity percentages imply n81 not n82 (Methods, Participants)
findings.description: The sentence states 82 participants, but only one of the four race/ethnicity percentages (4.9%) is attainable as a share of 82. All four are simultaneously attainable at exactly one denominator in the searched range: 81. The most likely innocent explanation is straightforward and should be stated first -- one participant did not report race/ethnicity, so the percentages were computed over the 81 who did. findings.title: Stalt thresholded p not concealing
findings.description: Rulebook rule 2 asks whether a thresholded p conceals an extreme value. It does not here, for a reason worth stating plainly: the paper PRINTS the chi-square statistic beside every thresholded p, so nothing is hidden -- the exact p is recoverable by any reader, as this check just did. An eleven-order-of-magnitude gap is simply what a chi-square of 65 on 4,589 observations produces, and style rules require reporting it as a floor. The same reasoning covers the other seven thresholded p-values in the paper. Correct reporting, not a finding.

findings.notes: FAMILY DEFINITION IS DOING A LOT OF WORK HERE AND THE CAVEAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE NUMBER. The family I supplied is broad -- every significance test in the Results -- and under it both results significant at exact p (.02 and .02, the two life-satisfaction models) fall below every correction threshold. But those two are not independent claims: they are the SAME cognitive well-being outcome fitted with and without a loneliness covariate, so counting them as two is already generous. Under the narrower and quite defensible family of two primary outcomes, Bonferroni alpha is .025 and the cognitive result at p=.02 survives. The affective result is untouched under any reading: at chi-square 28.90 its true p is around 8e-08, orders of magnitude below any threshold. The honest statement is that the paper's FIRST headline claim is robust to multiplicity and its SECOND is fragile to it, and that the paper applies and mentions no correction anywhere. One further, unquantifiable factor: at least twelve moderation tests and two interaction tests are reported only as 'ps > .16' and 'ps > .44', and two more sit in the supplements, so the true comparison count exceeds the fifteen counted here. This is a FLOOR on the multiplicity problem.

findings.title: Abstract null moderation claims unbounded (Abstract; Results, Moderation)
findings.description: 'Not significant' is not 'no effect'. With an analytic n around 77 and between-person moderators, the study has low power to detect moderation, so a minimum p of .16 is entirely compatible with moderating effects large enough to matter. Because no interval is printed, the largest moderating effect still consistent with these data cannot be computed -- by me or by any reader. The abstract states the null as a positive finding, which is the strongest form the claim can take and the one least supported by what is reported. A reporting-practice finding with no arithmetic in it, so nothing is missing from the toolkit here.

findings.title: Interaction beta larger than headline beta
findings.description: Two standardized coefficients of near-equal magnitude are reported with markedly different t statistics, in models fitted to the same participants. There is a completely ordinary explanation and it is probably the right one: the second model adds an apparently uncentred Facebook-use x direct-contact product term, and the resulting collinearity inflates the standard error of every term involving it, which is exactly how a sizeable beta ends up with a small t. I record this as INDETERMINATE rather than as a flag because I cannot distinguish that from a transcription error in the beta without the standard errors -- and the standard errors are precisely what Text S3 was cited to provide and does

findings.title: Analytic n never stated
findings.description: The paper reports the observation count (4,589) but never the participant count entering the OLS life-satisfaction models; a reader must infer it from the degrees of freedom. The df chain is at least self-consistent, stepping down by one per added covariate exactly as it should, which is a point in the paper's favour -- and I used that chain as my working n elsewhere in this sweep, labelling it an inference every time. Recorded as indeterminate because the figure is genuinely absent rather than wrong. It matters because Table 1's correlations, the twelve moderation tests and all three OLS models depend on an n the reader is never told.

findings.title: No power analysis reported (Methods, Participants)
findings.description: No a-priori power analysis and no sample-size justification appear anywhere. This is unremarkable for a 2013 experience-sampling paper and is NOT offered as a criticism of the authors' conduct; it is recorded because it bears directly on the moderation nulls above. The participant-level tests run on roughly 77 people and the paper itself describes its effects as 'small', so the twelve null moderation tests are where an unstated power assumption does the most work.
